caption_hook: Oklahoma has a lava-capped mesa, gypsum caves and granite older than most mountains.

layers.name: BLACK MESA BASALT
layers.hook: A lava cap on the high point
layers.what: Lava from volcanoes in New Mexico flowed across the Panhandle and cooled into hard black rock. It now caps Black Mesa, the highest ground in Oklahoma.
layers.bonus: The mesa top is 4,973 feet high, higher than any other spot in the state.

layers.name: MORRISON FORMATION
layers.what: The same river mud that makes Colorado famous also reaches the tip of Oklahoma. Bones of long-necked sauropods have been dug from it near Kenton. Its colorful mud layers are easy to spot on the mesa slopes.
layers.bonus: The Panhandle sits at the edge of Morrison country, which stretches north to Montana.

layers.name: BLAINE FORMATION
layers.what: A salty sea dried out across this part of Oklahoma, leaving thick beds of gypsum and salt. Water later dissolved long caves in the soft rock, like Alabaster Caverns.
layers.bonus: Alabaster Caverns is one of the largest natural gypsum caves open to the public.

layers.name: ARBUCKLE GROUP
layers.hook: A tropical reef under the south
layers.what: Thick limestone built up in a warm shallow sea in the Cambrian and Ordovician. It is folded into the Arbuckle Mountains, where Turner Falls spills over it.
layers.bonus: Turner Falls is the tallest waterfall in Oklahoma, at 77 feet.

layers.name: MOUNT SCOTT GRANITE
layers.what: When the continent started to split apart, molten rock welled up and cooled into pink granite. The Wichita Mountains are its worn-down stumps. Hikers can scramble over the bare pink boulders.
layers.bonus: Mount Scott rises 2,464 feet, and a wild bison herd roams the refuge below it.
